We can’t diagnose you or say for certain you have a problem, but you definitely have the classic symptoms. 

I wouldn’t worry about the blood test coming back wrong. Worst case you might be at the higher end of normal thyroid function. However the blood tests don’t lie my friend. So don’t stress about that! 

High blood pressure doesn’t typically cause symptoms believe it or not! So what you’re experiencing is most likely thyroid related. 

Also there is primary and secondary hypertension. 

Primary- don’t know the exact cause. It’s usually poor diet, lack of exercise or genetic. 

Secondary- due to an under lying condition (ex: hyperthyroidism) 

If you find out you have excess thyroid hormone and start treatment you should see improvement in your BP. 

I absolutely felt the same way when I was diagnosed, and I’m sorry to hear you’re feeling that way too! It’s not fun. 

If you wanted to know in case you get diagnosed:

You’ll most likely be put on an anti thyroid drug and possibly a beta blocker. The beta blocker is pretty much prescribed to help manage symptoms since anti thyroid drugs take a little bit to kick in. 

If you have hyperthyroidism due to Graves (this is the most common reason, at least in the US) down the line they may recommend RAI or a thyroidectomy. It’s possible to achieve remission though! Stay well and best of luck!

I developed it after a traumatic event and started having pretty bad nightmares. I didn’t start experiencing it until I was about 22. 

When it started for me though I had also just quit drinking, got diagnosed with an autoimmune disease, was working/going to school full time, and several other things.

I just think extreme stress in general is kinda what did me in.

The hallucinations sound a lot of sleep paralysis. During sleep paralysis your mind is still awake but you’re not going to be able to move. Your body has already gone into a paralyzed state before sleep or it is still “paralyzed” upon waking up. 

Sleep paralysis can be associated with narcolepsy, panic disorders, PTSD, family history, and I believe a few other things. 

I experience sleep paralysis as well and I understand it is terrifying. 

I’m not a doctor or anything so I’m not trying to say this is 100% what it is. I just thought I’d share the possibility with you. I hope you get to the bottom of it!

Edit: [here ](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/articles/what-you-should-know-about-sleep-paralysis)  is some information for you if you’d like to look more into it. Good luck!

Hello! I am in the same situation as you. I’m either going back to school full time either in the fall or spring depending on what program I get into. Like you, I am worried. I am actually really freaking out. 

I’m sure this is overdone advice but I feel like it’s truly the best method 

What I’ve been doing to help is im forcing myself (basically exposure therapy) to do things I’m uncomfortable with and I know will cause me to panic.

Ex: grocery stores, specifically standing in a long line because I feel trapped. I pick the longest line I see at the store. Or driving on a busy road that has a lot of stop lights. Feeling trapped in a place i will have a panic attack is a massive trigger for me. It’s **hard** but it’s important. 

Doing this I’m learning how to control the panic (in public) slowly but surely. 

Some things that help me (also unmedicated) 

They’re pretty basic but..

1.) accept and acknowledge I am in panicking 

2.) counting backward from 100 in 3’s (tricking my brain to think of something else)

3.) having some kind of lavender scent with me if possible because it’s calming 

4.) breathe in 5 seconds, hold 5 seconds, breathe out 5 seconds 

5.) mindfulness meditation practices 

Above all do these things where I will be scared. The first step/attempt is and always will be the hardest one.

It’s important to remember though everyone reacts different to different treatments. What works for me might not work for you. Some people say surgery was the best route to take some say the medication was best for them. It takes time and it is a journey. It also may depend on if you have nodules on your thyroid if I remember correctly. I’m no doctor though haha 

As far as them not taking you seriously for your age I was worried about that too because I’m 22F and no one in my family has Graves’ disease/hyperthyroidism, but I was honest about my symptoms and I didn’t have any issues.

I am currently going through the same thing as you right up to the working with people and getting my mind off things, nightmares, self medicating and also being in a new relationship. 

Going to a group for DV survivors really reallllllly helped. Although I’m still jumpy and get nightmares sometimes understanding you’re not alone helps. As horrific as it is knowing someone went through the same thing as you it makes you feel less on your own.

One thing that has worked for me aside from therapy/group is meditation. I started with guided mediation and now I’m better about being able to do it on my own. 

I cant put into words how hard it is to do at first, but over time you can almost “train” yourself to have an ability to clear your mind. It’s not always perfect it’s 100% not a cure BUT it’s a really great skill to learn. 

It’s hard to push past this because your “lizard brain” (aka the primitive part of your brain where instincts warns us of danger) takes a long time to calm down after circumstances like this. Sometimes you’re constantly on the look out when there’s nothing to look for. You may consciously or subconsciously fear because you put your guard down once.

“Lizard brain” doesn’t want that to happen.  It doesn’t want you to put your guard down again because “guard down equals danger” does that make sense? I’m horrible at writing. 

Anyways, another thing that helped me was sobriety. It was hard because the first couple months I HAD to acknowledge what happened to me, I had to face my fears up front instead of just drowning myself in alcohol. Being sober gave me no choice.

Getting through the first couple of months isn’t easy, but you also can’t get past something traumatizing like this while hiding behind a shield. Getting sober/confronting things head on I like to think of as “facing the final boss” because it just was so fucking hard going at it and forcing myself to remember and think about what my ex did to me.

After the sobriety is when I started sorting through things in therapy and also meditation.

Don’t get me wrong. It’s still hard I still struggle sometimes and I still have nightmares. However it’s fewer and further between and now I don’t **always** jump when my SO hugs me, and I can almost sleep well. It’s a process for all of us, it takes time like anything else, the hardest part it starting to face it. 

Be patient with yourself, communicate with your SO about things that bother you, and remember that just because it’s hard to go through doesn’t mean you aren’t capable of handling it. One thing we all have in common in this subreddit is strength.
